title: The King's Gambit
subtitle: A Romantic-era pawn sacrifice for the center and the f-file
summary: White sacrifices the f-pawn on move two to seize the center and rip open the f-file for a rook, trading long-term material for a fast attack -- at the real risk of leaving the king exposed for the rest of the game.

rootAnnotations.title: A pawn for the center and the f-file
rootAnnotations.body: 2.f4 offers a pawn so that, after ...exf4, White can meet e5 with a full center (d4/e4) and use the open f-file against f7. It was the favorite weapon of the Romantic era. The cost is real: White's king cannot castle kingside until the f-file is resolved, so any slow or inaccurate play can leave it dangerously exposed.

annotations.title: The gambit pawn
annotations.body: White offers the f-pawn to divert Black's e-pawn, aiming to answer ...exf4 with d4, building a big center while the f-file stands open for a rook.
Accepting is the most direct test of the gambit: Black banks the extra pawn and dares White to prove enough compensation. This is the King's Gambit Accepted.

annotations.title: King's Gambit Declined
annotations.body: Black ignores the offer and develops naturally instead, keeping a healthy structure and sidestepping the sharp theoretical battles of the Accepted lines. It is a calm, practical way to meet the gambit without memorizing forcing variations.

annotations.title: Stopping ...Qh4+
annotations.body: Before anything else, White must prevent 3...Qh4+, which would drag the king to e2 and cost the right to castle. Nf3 covers h4 and develops at the same time -- nearly every King's Gambit Accepted line starts here.

annotations.title: The Modern Defense
annotations.body: Rather than clinging to the extra pawn with 3...g5, Black strikes back in the center immediately. This is considered Black's most reliable answer: it returns the pawn but neutralizes White's central and attacking ideas.

annotations.title: Holding the extra pawn
annotations.body: The old main line: Black defends f4 and hangs on to the extra pawn. It leads to razor-sharp positions like the Kieseritzky and Muzio Gambits, where both kings can come under fire -- rewarding preparation and punishing the unprepared on either side.

annotations.title: Eyeing f7 again
annotations.body: As in the Italian Game, the bishop heads straight for f7, keeping pressure on the position while Black's king is still in the center.

Black recaptures and centralizes the knight. Material is now roughly level for the moment (White is still missing the f-pawn), but White's pieces are far more active than in a normal opening at this stage.

annotations.title: Development finished, compensation banked
annotations.body: Castling completes development and finally tucks the king away -- the single most important task in any gambit. White is a pawn down but ahead in development with open lines toward f7; the whole opening was played to reach exactly this kind of position quickly.
